lesson.title: The Errors Python Won't Even Try to Run
lesson.summary: A syntax error means your code breaks Python's grammar rules, and Python catches it by reading through the whole file before running a single line, refusing to start at all.
lesson.body:
The overview chapter described three categories of broken code, and this chapter goes deep on the first one: the syntax error. Before Python executes anything, it first reads your entire file and checks whether it follows Python's grammar, a step called parsing. If parsing finds something that does not match a valid Python structure, Python stops immediately and reports a SyntaxError, and this is the defining trait that separates a syntax error from the other two categories: it is always caught before the program runs, not partway through it. Not even the lines before the mistake get executed, because Python never starts running the program at all until the whole file has parsed successfully.

Common causes are almost always small, mechanical slips rather than deep logical mistakes: forgetting the colon at the end of an if, for, while, or def line; leaving a parenthesis, bracket, or quotation mark unclosed; using inconsistent indentation; or accidentally using one of Python's reserved keywords, like for or class, as a variable name. Here is a real example, a function definition missing its closing colon.

```python
def greet(name)
    print("Hello, " + name)
```

Trying to run this file prints:

```
SyntaxError: expected ':'
```

along with a pointer showing roughly where in the offending line the parser got confused, right after name where a colon should have appeared. Notice what this error report does not include: there is no traceback showing a chain of function calls, because the program never actually started running. A syntax error is purely about the shape of the text, whether it forms a legal Python program at all, and has nothing to do with what values or data the program would have worked with had it been allowed to run.

This has a practical upside. Because a syntax error is caught before execution and does not depend on any particular input or data, it is completely reproducible: the exact same broken file will fail to run the exact same way every single time, and most code editors can even flag many syntax errors while you are still typing, before you ever try to run the file. When you see SyntaxError, resist the urge to look for a subtle logic mistake. Look instead at the punctuation and structure right around the reported location: a missing colon, an unclosed bracket, or a misplaced quotation mark is almost always sitting there.
